identity.title: Safety Alignment Should be Made More Than Just a Few Tokens Deep

problem.claim: Explain and mitigate vulnerabilities in LLM safety alignment, including jailbreaks from simple attacks or benign fine-tuning.

gap.claim: Existing safety alignment can take a shortcut by adapting generation mainly over the first few output tokens, a shared issue the authors call shallow safety alignment.

contributions.claim: Introduces the consolidated notion of shallow safety alignment to explain multiple LLM vulnerabilities.
Presents case studies linking shallow safety alignment to adversarial suffix, prefilling, decoding-parameter, and fine-tuning attacks.
Investigates deeper alignment and proposes a regularized fine-tuning objective that constrains updates on initial tokens.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors' stated key contribution is using shallow safety alignment as a consolidated notion that reveals promising mitigation directions.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that deepening safety alignment beyond the first few tokens meaningfully improves robustness against some common exploits.
The authors report designing a regularized fine-tuning objective intended to make safety alignment more persistent against fine-tuning attacks by constraining initial-token updates.
The authors report that shallow safety alignment contributes to several recently discovered vulnerabilities across four listed attack types.

narrative_sequence.summary: Safety alignment is described as vulnerable, including to simple attacks and benign fine-tuning.
The paper identifies a shortcut focused on the first few output tokens and names it shallow safety alignment.
Case studies connect the notion to multiple attack vulnerabilities.
The paper reports deeper alignment and a regularized objective as mitigation directions.

source_observation.claim: The paper groups several attack vulnerabilities under one mechanism-level diagnosis: alignment concentrated in the first few output tokens.

lessons.interpretation: A unifying mechanism can make a scattered vulnerability landscape easier to analyze and connect to targeted interventions.
lessons.application: When presenting multiple failure modes, define a shared mechanism and map each failure mode to it before proposing mitigations.
lessons.exception: Do not use this structure when the abstract does not support a common mechanism across the cases.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify which exploits improve, the magnitude of improvement, or evaluation conditions.
It does not report comparative baselines, model details, or quantitative results for the regularized objective.
